topic: How Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) in Transformers Store Facts
target_audience: University students in Computer Science or AI enthusiasts with basic linear algebra knowledge

sections.title: The Mystery of Model Memory
sections.content: Introduce the central question: When you ask a Transformer 'What is the capital of France?', where is that specific fact retrieved from? Differentiate between the 'Attention Mechanism' (which handles context/relationships) and the 'MLP Layers' (which act as the model's long-term memory or 'knowledge base').
sections.example: An animation showing a detective (the model) searching a library. The Attention mechanism is the detective's flashlight looking at surrounding words, while the MLP is the bookshelf containing the encyclopedia of facts.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The MLP Architecture Review
sections.content: Briefly revisit the structure of a standard MLP block in a Transformer: an input vector, a first linear layer (W1), a non-linear activation (ReLU/GELU), and a second linear layer (W2). Establish the concept of 'activation' as a signal that a specific pattern has been recognized.
sections.example: A visual diagram showing a vector 'v' entering a gate. If 'v' matches a pattern in W1, the gate opens (activation), allowing a specific signal to pass through to W2.

sections.title: The Key-Value Memory Analogy
sections.content: Explain the 'Key-Value' hypothesis. Each neuron in the MLP's hidden layer acts as a 'Key' (stored in W1) that recognizes a specific concept, and its corresponding weights in W2 act as the 'Value' (the information to be added back to the hidden state).
sections.example: Visualizing W1 as a 'Key' that looks for the concept 'City: Paris' and W2 as the 'Value' that outputs the attribute 'Country: France'.

sections.title: Mathematical Visualization: The Dot Product Match
sections.content: Present the math: The input hidden state 'x' is multiplied by a row in W1 (the key vector 'ki'). Use a heat map animation to show that if the dot product (x · ki) is high, the neuron 'fires'. This represents 'recognizing' the fact trigger.
sections.example: Show a vector for 'Eiffel Tower' aligning perfectly with a 'Paris' key vector in W1, causing the 'Value' in W2 to inject 'Location: France' into the model's processing stream.

sections.title: Fact Retrieval in Action
sections.content: Demonstrate the full workflow of fact retrieval. 1. Input processing. 2. Pattern matching in the hidden layer (W1). 3. Information extraction from the output layer (W2). 4. Integration into the residual stream.
sections.example: Input text: 'The iPhone was created by...'. The MLP layer activates a 'Knowledge Neuron' for 'Apple Inc.' and 'Steve Jobs', which then updates the sentence representation to predict the next word.

sections.title: Summary: The Global Knowledge Map
sections.content: Conclude by explaining that a Transformer contains thousands of these 'Key-Value' pairs across many layers. Some layers store low-level linguistic patterns, while deeper layers store complex factual knowledge. Summarize why this makes MLPs the 'Flash Drive' of the Transformer.
sections.example: A zoom-out animation showing a 3D grid of neurons, where different clusters glow when the model is asked about History, Science, or Geography, visualizing the model's internal 'map of knowledge'.
